en: Thus have I heard: the *Anuruddhasutta*, the 127th discourse of the *Majjhima Nikāya*.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga addressed a certain man:
“Come, good man, go to where the Venerable Anuruddha is; having approached him, pay homage with your head at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha in my name, saying:”
“Venerable sir, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha with his head.
And please say this:
‘Venerable sir, may the Venerable Anuruddha consent to take a meal tomorrow together with three others at the home of the carpenter Pañcakaṅga.’”
“Venerable sir, it would be well if the Venerable Anuruddha were to come earlier;
for the master carpenter Pañcakaṅga has many duties and much work to do on account of the king’s business.
“Very well, venerable sir,” that man replied to the master carpenter Pañcakaṅga and went to where the Venerable Anuruddha was.
He approached him; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Anuruddha and sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, that man said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Venerable sir, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga pays homage with his head at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha and says this:"
“Venerable sir, may the Venerable Anuruddha please accept tomorrow’s meal from the householder Pañcakaṅga, with himself as the fourth guest.
And may the Venerable Anuruddha come somewhat earlier, venerable sir,
for the householder Pañcakaṅga has many duties and much to do on account of his royal service.”
The Venerable Anuruddha consented by remaining silent.

Then, when that night had passed, the Venerable Anuruddha dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of Pañcakaṅga the steward; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga, with his own hands, served and satisfied the Venerable Anuruddha with various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft.
When the Venerable Anuruddha had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga took a low seat and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Here, Bhante, elder bhikkhus approached me and said:
‘Householder, develop the immeasurable liberation of mind.
Some elders spoke thus:”
“‘Householder, develop the exalted liberation of mind.
Now, venerable sir, as for this immeasurable liberation of mind and this exalted liberation of mind—
are these states different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning and different only in phrasing?”
“In that case, householder, let what occurs to you here be spoken; for from this, there will be no uncertainty for you.
“Venerable sir, it has occurred to me thus:
‘This immeasurable liberation of mind and this exalted liberation of mind—these states are one in meaning, differing only in expression.’”
“Householder, this immeasurable liberation of mind and this exalted liberation of mind—these phenomena differ both in meaning and in phrasing.
Householder, this can be understood through this method of exposition as to how these phenomena differ both in meaning and in phrasing.
And what, householder, is the immeasurable liberation of mind?”
"Here, householder, a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,
likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself,
he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity."
He dwells pervading [the world] with a mind free from ill will;
with a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy…
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third,
and likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—
vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
"This, householder, is called the immeasurable liberation of mind.
And what, householder, is the exalted liberation of mind?
Here, householder, a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as exalted as far as a single tree-root."
"This, householder, is called the exalted liberation of mind.
Furthermore, householder, here a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon two or three tree roots as 'exalted.
This too, householder, is called the exalted liberation of mind."
Furthermore, householder, here a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon an entire village field as "lofty.
This too, householder, is called the lofty liberation of mind.
Furthermore, householder, here a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon two or three village fields as "lofty."
This too, householder, is called the exalted liberation of mind.
Furthermore, householder, here a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as exalted an area as great a kingdom as there is.
This too, householder, is called the exalted liberation of mind.
Furthermore, householder, here a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon two or three great kingdoms as "lofty.
This too, householder, is called the lofty liberation of mind.
Furthermore, householder, here a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon the earth as far as the ocean’s edge as "lofty."
“This too, householder, is called the exalted liberation of mind.
It is by this method, householder, that it should be understood how these phenomena differ both in meaning and in phrasing.
Now, householder, there are these four modes of rebirth.”
Which four?
Here, householder, a certain person dwells having pervaded [the world] with the thought, "It is limited light," and having resolved upon it.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of Limited Light.
Furthermore, householder, here someone dwells having pervaded and resolved with the thought, ‘immeasurable radiance.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of immeasurable radiance.
Furthermore, householder, here someone dwells having pervaded and resolved with the thought, ‘corrupted radiance.’
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of Defiled Radiance.
But here, householder, someone else dwells having pervaded and resolved upon the thought, "It is pure radiance.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of Pure Radiance.
"These, householder, are the four modes of rebirth into existence.

There comes a time, householder, when those deities gather together in one place; when they have gathered together in one place, a diversity of color is perceived among them, but not a diversity of radiance.
It is just as if, householder, a man were to bring many oil lamps into a single house."
When they have entered one house, their diversity of color is indeed perceived, but not their diversity of radiance.

In the same way, householder, there comes a time when those deities assemble together; when they have assembled together, their diversity of color is indeed perceived, but not their diversity of radiance.
There also comes a time, householder, when those deities depart from there; as they depart from there, both their diversity of color and their diversity of radiance are perceived.
"Just as if, householder, a man were to take those many oil lamps out from that house; when they have been taken out from there,
a diversity of flames and a diversity of lights would be discerned—
even so, householder, there comes a time when those deities depart from there, and as they depart from there, a diversity of complexions and a diversity of lights are discerned."
"Householder, it does not occur to those deities:
'This is permanent for us,' or 'It is stable,' or 'It is eternal. Rather, wherever those deities become attached, there they find delight.
Just as, householder, when flies are being carried along by a yoke or a basket, it does not occur to them:"
‘This is ours: permanent, stable, or eternal. Yet, wherever those flies settle, right there they find delight.
In the same way, householder, it does not occur to those deities:
‘This is ours: permanent, stable, or eternal. Yet, wherever those deities settle, right there they find delight.”
When this was said, the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Excellent, Bhante Anuruddha.
But there is something further that I wish to ask about this."
“Venerable sir, as for those deities who are radiant, are they all of limited radiance, or are there some among them who have immeasurable radiance?
“In that respect, friend Kaccāna, there are some deities here who are of limited radiance, and there are also some deities here who have immeasurable radiance.

“But what, venerable Anuruddha, is the cause, what is the reason, why among those deities who have been reborn in the same divine realm, some are of limited radiance while others have immeasurable radiance?”
“Therefore, friend Kaccāna, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.
What do you think, friend Kaccāna:

when a bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon a single tree-root as ‘lofty,’ does he dwell having pervaded the entire world-sphere with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from enmity and ill will?”
“And as for this bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon two or three tree roots as ‘lofty’—
of these two developments of the mind, which development of the mind is loftier?
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon two or three tree roots as ‘lofty’— ”
“This is the more exalted of these two developments of mind.
“What do you think, friend Kaccāna?
Suppose a bhikkhu, having pervaded and resolved upon as ‘exalted’ as many as two or three tree roots...”
“...dwells; and there is this other bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon an entire village field as ‘lofty’—of these two developments of mind, which development of mind is more lofty?
“The one, venerable sir, who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon an entire village field as ‘lofty’—”
“This [latter] development of mind is more exalted than these two.

“What do you think, friend Kaccāna: Is that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon a single village district as ‘exalted,’ or that bhikkhu who [dwells having pervaded and resolved upon] two or three village districts?”
“Regarding ‘the exalted’: one dwells having pervaded and resolved upon it as ‘exalted.
Of these two developments of the mind, which development of the mind is more exalted?
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as far as two or three village districts as ‘exalted’—”
“This [latter] is the more exalted of these two developments of the mind.

“What do you think, friend Kaccāna: between that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as ‘exalted’ as far as two or three village districts, and that bhikkhu who [dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as ‘exalted’] as far as one great kingdom...”
“Regarding ‘the exalted’: when one dwells having pervaded and resolved upon this, which of these two developments of the mind is more exalted?
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as ‘exalted’ even a single great kingdom—”
“Of these two developments of the mind, this one is more exalted.

“What do you think, friend Kaccāna? Between that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as ‘exalted’ a single great kingdom, and that bhikkhu who [dwells having pervaded and resolved upon as ‘exalted’] two or three great kingdoms...”
“Between these two developments of the mind— one who dwells having pervaded and resolved with the thought ‘lofty’ as far as two or three great kingdoms— which development of the mind is more lofty?
“Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved with the thought ‘lofty’ as far as two or three great kingdoms— ”
“This [latter] development of mind is more exalted than these two.
“What do you think, friend Kaccāna? There is a bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved with the thought ‘exalted’ as far as two or three great realms;
and there is a bhikkhu who [dwells having pervaded and resolved with the thought ‘exalted’] as far as the ocean’s edge...”
“Of these two developments of the mind— one who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon the earth as ‘lofty’ (mahaggata),

and one who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon the earth as far as the ocean’s edge as ‘lofty’— which of these two developments of the mind is loftier? “Venerable sir, that bhikkhu who dwells having pervaded and resolved upon the earth as far as the ocean’s edge as ‘lofty’— ”
“Which of these two developments of mind is more exalted?

“This, friend Kaccāna, is the cause, this is the reason why, among those deities who have been reborn in a single divine realm, some deities there are of Limited Radiance, while other deities there are of Immeasurable Radiance.
“Excellent, Bhante Anuruddha!”
"But there is something further that I wish to ask regarding this:
Venerable sir, as for all those deities who possess radiant light, are they all defiled in their radiance, or are there some among them who possess pure radiance?
"In part, friend Kaccāna, there are some deities here who possess defiled radiance; however, there are also some among them who possess pure radiance."
“Venerable Anuruddha, what is the cause, what is the reason, why among those deities who have been reborn in a single divine assembly,
some deities here are of defiled radiance while others here are of pure radiance?
“In that case, friend Kaccāna, I shall give you a simile.”
By means of a simile, some wise persons understand the meaning of what has been said.
Just as, friend Kaccāna, when an oil lamp is burning, if both the oil and the wick are impure,
it burns dimly because the oil is impure and the wick is impure.
In the same way, friend Kaccāna, here a certain bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon the thought, ‘It is defiled.
His bodily restlessness is not well pacified, his sloth and torpor are not well removed, and his restlessness and remorse are not well dispelled.

Because his bodily restlessness is not well pacified, because his sloth and torpor are not well removed, and because his restlessness and remorse are not well dispelled, he meditates as it were blindly.
Thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the devas of Defiled Radiance.
Just as, friend Kaccāna, when an oil lamp is burning, the oil is pure and the wick is pure, because the oil is pure and the wick is pure, it does not burn with a flickering flame; so too...
In the same way, friend Kaccāna, here a certain bhikkhu dwells having pervaded and resolved upon [the thought]:
"It is completely pure. His bodily rigidity is well-allayed, his sloth and torpor are thoroughly eradicated, and his restlessness and remorse are well-removed.
Because his bodily rigidity is well-allayed, because his sloth and torpor are thoroughly eradicated, and because his restlessness and remorse are well-removed, he does not meditate as if blind.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods of Pure Radiance.

This, friend Kaccāna, is the cause, this is the reason why, among those deities who have been reborn in a single divine realm, some deities there are of defiled radiance, while others there are of pure radiance.
When this was said, the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said this to the Venerable Anuruddha:
“Excellent, venerable Anuruddha!
Venerable Anuruddha does not say,
‘Thus have I heard,’ nor does he say, ‘It ought to be thus.’”
"But nevertheless, Bhante, the Venerable Anuruddha speaks of those deities only as ‘such-and-such deities’ and ‘so-and-so deities.
It occurs to me, Bhante:
‘Surely the Venerable Anuruddha must have previously lived together with those deities, conversed with them, and engaged in discussion with them.’"
“Surely, friend Kaccāna, this speech was spoken by you out of malice and with intent to insult;
nevertheless, I shall explain it to you:
‘Friend Kaccāna, for a long time I have previously lived together with those deities, conversed with them, and engaged in discussion with them.’”
When this was said, the Venerable Sabhiya Kaccāna said this to the carpenter Pañcakanga:
"It is a gain for you, householder;
it is well-gained by you, householder, that you yourself have abandoned that state of doubt, and that we have obtained this exposition of the Dhamma to hear."
The Anuruddhasutta, the seventh, is finished.
